title: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle
public_title: Why do your friends leave when the fun stops? | Aristotle
hook: You think your closest friends will stick around when life gets hard.
source_kind: Original commentary on the retained original public-domain text; modern examples identified and limitations discussed; owner review required

source_passages.excerpt: The clearest illustration is perhaps the case of the gods, because they are most superior in all good things.

However, let us drop these questions, because they are in fact somewhat foreign to our purpose.
So then it appears that all the instances of Communion are parts of the great Social one: and corresponding Friendships will follow upon such Communions.
Of these the best is Monarchy, and Timocracy the worst.
Well, these are generally the changes to which the various Constitutions are liable, being the least in degree and the easiest to make.
These friendships are also between superiors and inferiors, for which reason parents are not merely loved but also honoured.

sections.title: Section 1: Modern humans seek perfect, selfless bonds, but a
sections.narration: You think your closest friends will stick around when life gets hard. Yet ancient thinkers actually saw divine perfection as impossible for mortals. Researchers at the Survey Center on American Life studied this in 2021. The result? Twelve percent of adults now report having zero close friends. We expect modern relationships to be completely selfless and eternal. But real life often forces people apart over time. Cornwell and his team at Cornell University proved this in 2008. They found that average social networks drop by seventeen percent every decade after early adulthood. Aristotle understood this human limitation over two thousand years ago. He realized that true perfection belongs only to higher beings, not to us. As Aristotle wrote, "The clearest illustration is perhaps the case of the gods, because they are most superior in all good things." Humans simply cannot maintain perfect bonds forever. We must change how we view our everyday friendships.

sections.title: Section 2: We feel betrayed when transactional friendships f
sections.narration: We feel deeply betrayed when our closest friends vanish during hard times. But Aristotle saw this coming centuries ago. He argued that most human bonds rely purely on utility or pleasure. Think of a gym partner who disappears the moment you stop going, or a coworker who ghosted you after changing jobs. Aristotle wrote: "Those connected by motives of profit, or pleasure, hold together somewhat longer: so long, that is to say, as they can give pleasure or profit mutually." When the mutual benefit ends, the connection naturally breaks apart. Is this transactional pattern just a modern problem? Data shows our social circles naturally shrink as we age anyway. Researchers at Cornell University found social network size drops by seventeen percent every decade after early adulthood. We confuse temporary companions with lifelong soulmates. We expect deep loyalty from people who only joined us for the fun. Realizing this truth protects your heart from constant disappointment.

sections.title: Section 3: We obsess over fixing broken relationships, but d
sections.narration: We spend endless energy trying to fix broken bonds. We feel guilty when people drift away. Think about keeping old clothes that no longer fit. Holding onto every friendship is just like crowding your closet with things you cannot wear. It only creates unnecessary clutter in your daily life. Aristotle says some ties should end. Not every bond deserves your time. Cornwell and colleagues found in 2008 that social networks shrink fast. Your circle drops by seventeen percent every decade after early adulthood. That's it. It is a natural part of growing up. You do not need to save every connection. "However, let us drop these questions, because they are in fact somewhat foreign to our purpose." Focus on real virtue instead. Let shallow ties fade without remorse. You simply cannot maintain fifty close relationships at once. Accept these honest limits. Clearing out dead weight brings true peace to your mind.

sections.title: Section 4: Modern isolation feels individual, but ancient ph
sections.narration: You might think modern loneliness is just a personal failure. In a 2021 Survey Center on American Life report, twelve percent of adults reported having no close friends at all. But Aristotle saw friendship as a deeply public matter. Your personal bonds connect directly to the health of your entire community. Small groups form the bedrock of a stable society. When your inner circle fractures, the whole city suffers. Why does getting older make it so much harder to stay connected? A 2008 Cornell study showed social network size drops seventeen percent every decade after early adulthood. As Aristotle wrote, "So then it appears that all the instances of Communion are parts of the great Social one: and corresponding Friendships will follow upon such Communions." Isolated people cannot build a strong society. Your personal ties shape the broader civic world. Cultivating real virtue in your relationships strengthens the entire community around you.

sections.title: Section 5: We struggle with toxic social hierarchies, which
sections.narration: You can see this link between personal ties and society in Aristotle's political ideas. He believed a healthy state reflects healthy human connections. Good systems protect the public good. Corrupt systems only serve the leaders in power. Aristotle ranked these political forms in order of quality. He wrote, "Of these the best is Monarchy, and Timocracy the worst." Corrupt systems destroy trust. They create toxic social hierarchies where people use each other. Think of a bad landlord who exploits tenants instead of fixing broken heat. Modern isolation reflects this decay. Cornwell and colleagues at Cornell University in 2008 studied social connections over time. They found that network size drops by about seventeen percent every decade after early adulthood. Corrupt systems isolate individuals. They turn citizens into competitors. When you build honest relationships, you fight this trend. You build a stable micro-community around yourself. Real virtue resists toxic social hierarchies.

sections.title: Section 6: Sudden social shifts feel chaotic, yet structural
sections.narration: Structural changes in relationships feel chaotic, but they happen very slowly over time. Why does your circle shrink so drastically as you grow older? Social network size typically drops by about seventeen percent every decade after early adulthood. Sudden social shifts are usually minor adjustments that stack up silently. Think about a wooden deck outside your house. A single rainy day will not rot the wood. Decades of small rainstorms slowly weaken the timber until a plank snaps under your feet. Aristotle understood how small shifts alter entire structures. He wrote: "Well, these are generally the changes to which the various Constitutions are liable, being the least in degree and the easiest to make." Your social circle changes just like those political constitutions. Tiny shifts in shared habits slowly rewrite the rules of your connection. You do not lose people in a single dramatic fight. You lose them through small, quiet changes in daily life. Most people never notice the foundation shifting until it collapses completely.

sections.title: Section 7: Unbalanced relationships cause stress today, yet
sections.narration: Modern studies show how fragile our adult connections really are. The Survey Center on American Life found that twelve percent of adults now have no close friends at all. Research from Cornell shows our social networks shrink by seventeen percent every decade after early adulthood. You might feel this when old college roommates slowly stop texting back after you move away for a new job. Aristotle understood that life naturally creates gaps between people. He noted that "These friendships are also between superiors and inferiors, for which reason parents are not merely loved but also honoured." Think about how a mentor at work cannot just be a regular beer buddy. Unequal relationships always create tension when we expect perfect balance. But clear respect allows these bonds to survive change without breaking. So next time you feel a friendship shifting, remember that real connection takes honest effort. You think your closest friends will stick around when life gets hard.
